claim: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) is the most common focal epilepsy in adults.
source: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) is the most common focal epilepsy in adults and is often refractory to medication.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about mTLE.

claim: mTLE is often refractory to medication.
source: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) is the most common focal epilepsy in adults and is often refractory to medication.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of mTLE.

claim: Resection of the epileptogenic focus represents the only curative therapy for mTLE.
source: So far, resection of the epileptogenic focus represents the only curative therapy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as current clinical practice.

claim: The extent of early hippocampal neurodegeneration translates to the severity of hippocampal sclerosis in chronic epilepsy.
source: Here, we show for the first time that the extent of early hippocampal neurodegeneration and progressive microstructural changes in the dentate gyrus translate to the severity of hippocampal sclerosis and seizure burden in chronic epilepsy.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by longitudinal MRI and histological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Progressive microstructural changes in the dentate gyrus translate to the severity of hippocampal sclerosis in chronic epilepsy.
source: Here, we show for the first time that the extent of early hippocampal neurodegeneration and progressive microstructural changes in the dentate gyrus translate to the severity of hippocampal sclerosis and seizure burden in chronic epilepsy.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by DWI data and histological correlations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Progressive microstructural changes in the dentate gyrus translate to seizure burden in chronic epilepsy.
source: Here, we show for the first time that the extent of early hippocampal neurodegeneration and progressive microstructural changes in the dentate gyrus translate to the severity of hippocampal sclerosis and seizure burden in chronic epilepsy.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between PC1 scores and seizure frequency shown in Figure 9.

claim: Structural MRI biomarkers reflect the extent of sclerosis in human hippocampi.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that structural MRI biomarkers reflect the extent of sclerosis in human hippocampi.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ex vivo DWI scans and histology on resected hippocampi from mTLE patients shown in Figure 7.

claim: MRI biomarkers may allow an early prognosis of disease severity in mTLE before its first clinical manifestations.
source: Our findings may allow an early prognosis of disease severity in mTLE before its first clinical manifestations, thus expanding the therapeutic window.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the predictive correlations found in the study.

claim: Epilepsy has a prevalence of about 1%.
source: Epilepsy is a devastating disease, with a prevalence of about 1%, which makes it one of the most common neurological disorders.
evidence: This is stated as established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy accounts for 40% of epilepsy in adults.
source: Of particular clinical significance is mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE), in which seizures arise from mesial temporal limbic structures, as it is the most frequent form of epilepsy in adults (40%) and particularly resistant to pharmacological treatment (Engel, 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Engel, 2001 as established knowledge.

claim: Hippocampal sclerosis is characterized by the loss of CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Hippocampal sclerosis (HS), characterized by the loss of CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells, gliosis and associated with granule cell dispersion (GCD), represents the most common pathological hallmark of intractable mTLE (Thom, 2014; Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Thom, 2014 and Walker, 2015 as established pathological knowledge.

claim: Hippocampal sclerosis is associated with gliosis.
source: Hippocampal sclerosis (HS), characterized by the loss of CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells, gliosis and associated with granule cell dispersion (GCD), represents the most common pathological hallmark of intractable mTLE (Thom, 2014; Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Thom, 2014 and Walker, 2015 as established pathological knowledge.

claim: Hippocampal sclerosis is associated with granule cell dispersion.
source: Hippocampal sclerosis (HS), characterized by the loss of CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells, gliosis and associated with granule cell dispersion (GCD), represents the most common pathological hallmark of intractable mTLE (Thom, 2014; Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Thom, 2014 and Walker, 2015 as established pathological knowledge.

claim: Hippocampal sclerosis represents the most common pathological hallmark of intractable mTLE.
source: Hippocampal sclerosis (HS), characterized by the loss of CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells, gliosis and associated with granule cell dispersion (GCD), represents the most common pathological hallmark of intractable mTLE (Thom, 2014; Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Thom, 2014 and Walker, 2015 as established knowledge.

claim: Hippocampal sclerosis can emerge secondary to status epilepticus.
source: HS can emerge secondary to an initial precipitating insult, e.g. status epilepticus (SE), head trauma, febrile seizures or limbic encephalitis (Engel, 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Engel, 2001 as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Not all mTLE patients remain seizure-free after resection of epileptogenic tissue.
source: To date, resection of the lesioned, epileptogenic tissue is the only therapeutic intervention. However, not all patients remain seizure-free (Ryvlin and Kahane, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Ryvlin and Kahane, 2005 as a known clinical outcome.

claim: Non-invasive MRI techniques have become an important method to identify sclerotic tissue as a biomarker in human mTLE patients.
source: In this context, non-invasive MRI techniques have become an important method to identify sclerotic tissue as a biomarker in both human patients (Gomes and Shinnar, 2011; Urbach et al., 2014) and rodent TLE models (Nehlig, 2011; Shultz et al., 2014; Sierra et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources as established practice.

claim: MRI identification of sclerotic tissue has been restricted to the chronic stage of epilepsy when seizures have already emerged.
source: Up to now, this has been, however, restricted to the chronic stage of epilepsy when seizures have already emerged.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current MRI applications.

claim: In mTLE patients, the period between the initial epileptogenic insult and chronic epilepsy spans many years.
source: In mTLE patients, the period between the initial epileptogenic insult and chronic epilepsy spans many years (Lukasiuk and Becker, 2014), severely hindering the search for and validation of predictive biomarkers in human studies.
evidence: This is cited from Lukasiuk and Becker, 2014 as established knowledge.

claim: In animal models, epileptogenesis can be induced within weeks to months.
source: Conversely, in animal models, epileptogenesis can be induced within weeks to months (Lévesque and Avoli, 2013), providing an excellent opportunity to identify putative anatomical and physiological biomarkers of epileptogenesis.
evidence: This is cited from Lévesque and Avoli, 2013 as established knowledge about animal models.

claim: The intrahippocampal kainate mouse model replicates the major features of human mTLE.
source: To address this issue, we applied longitudinal multi-modal MRI in the intrahippocampal kainate mouse model that replicates the major features of human mTLE (i.e. the development of HS and of spontaneous recurrent seizures during epileptogenesis; Bouilleret et al., 1999; Riban et al. (2002); Heinrich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources as established knowledge about the model.

claim: The extent of granule cell dispersion varied substantially across kainate-injected mice.
source: The extent of GCD (Figure 1A–C) and cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 1D,E) varied substantially across kainate-injected mice (nKA = 8), but was positively correlated with each other (Figure 1F; r² = 0.69, p<0.01).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The extent of cell death-associated microgliosis varied substantially across kainate-injected mice.
source: The extent of GCD (Figure 1A–C) and cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 1D,E) varied substantially across kainate-injected mice (nKA = 8), but was positively correlated with each other (Figure 1F; r² = 0.69, p<0.01).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Granule cell dispersion and cell death-associated microgliosis are positively correlated in kainate-injected mice.
source: The extent of GCD (Figure 1A–C) and cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 1D,E) varied substantially across kainate-injected mice (nKA = 8), but was positively correlated with each other (Figure 1F; r² = 0.69, p<0.01).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 1F with statistical significance.

claim: All epileptic mice showed robust granule cell dispersion indicated by an increase in the total GCL volume compared to non-epileptic mice.
source: All epileptic mice showed robust GCD indicated by an increase in the total GCL volume compared to non-epileptic mice (Figure 1H; non-epi.: 415.8 ± 9.6 * 106 µm³; epi.: 1379.0 ± 164.5 * 108 µm³, p<0.01) and a high spatial extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 1I; non-epi.: 563.8 ± 493.7 µm; epi.: 6965.0 ± 811.8 µm, p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1H with statistical significance.

claim: Epileptic mice showed a high spatial extent of cell death-associated microgliosis compared to non-epileptic mice.
source: All epileptic mice showed robust GCD indicated by an increase in the total GCL volume compared to non-epileptic mice (Figure 1H; non-epi.: 415.8 ± 9.6 * 106 µm³; epi.: 1379.0 ± 164.5 * 108 µm³, p<0.01) and a high spatial extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 1I; non-epi.: 563.8 ± 493.7 µm; epi.: 6965.0 ± 811.8 µm, p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1I with statistical significance.

claim: The first high-amplitude recurrent paroxysmal episodes were recorded consistently after approximately two weeks in kainate-injected mice.
source: The first high-amplitude recurrent paroxysmal episodes were recorded consistently after approximately two weeks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H; number of epileptic discharges, 1d: 0.014 ± 0.004; 0.5w: 0.002 ± 0.002; 1w: 0.036 ± 0.019; 2w: 0.240 ± 0.065, p<0.01 vs 1w; 3w: 0.274 ± 0.070, p<0.01 vs 1w).
evidence: This is demonstrated by longitudinal EEG recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H with statistical analysis.

claim: T2-weighted imaging revealed a biphasic rise in hippocampal T2 intensity, characterized by a transient increase at day 1, followed by a drop to baseline at day 4 and a subsequent increase at 8 days after SE.
source: T2-weighted imaging revealed a biphasic rise in hippocampal T2 intensity, characterized by a transient increase at day 1, followed by a drop to baseline at day 4 and a subsequent increase at 8 days after SE (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by longitudinal T2-weighted imaging shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The early increase of T2 intensity was observed in the dentate gyrus at 1 day after SE.
source: The early increase of T2 intensity was observed in the dentate gyrus (DG) (Figure 2I; 1d: 10.6%) and the CA1 region (Figure 2G; 1d: 26.9%; both p<0.001), whereas in the late phase it was restricted to the DG (8d: 7.8%; 31d: 7.9%, both p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2I with statistical significance.

claim: The early increase of T2 intensity was observed in the CA1 region at 1 day after SE.
source: The early increase of T2 intensity was observed in the dentate gyrus (DG) (Figure 2I; 1d: 10.6%) and the CA1 region (Figure 2G; 1d: 26.9%; both p<0.001), whereas in the late phase it was restricted to the DG (8d: 7.8%; 31d: 7.9%, both p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G with statistical significance.

claim: In the late phase, T2 intensity increase was restricted to the dentate gyrus.
source: The early increase of T2 intensity was observed in the dentate gyrus (DG) (Figure 2I; 1d: 10.6%) and the CA1 region (Figure 2G; 1d: 26.9%; both p<0.001), whereas in the late phase it was restricted to the DG (8d: 7.8%; 31d: 7.9%, both p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2I with statistical significance.

claim: T2 intensity in the CA1 region at 1 day following SE significantly correlated with cell death-associated microgliosis.
source: Importantly, 1 day following SE, T2 intensity in the CA1 region significantly correlated with cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 2H; r² = 0.88, p<0.001).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2H with statistical significance.

claim: Early and subsequent T2 hyperintensities in the dentate gyrus were related to the later degree of granule cell dispersion.
source: Similarly, in the DG both early (at 1 day) and subsequent T2 hyperintensities (at 8–31 days) were related to the later degree of GCD (Figure 2J).
evidence: This relationship is shown in Figure 2J through correlation analysis.

claim: NAA concentrations decreased substantially at 1 day following SE.
source: As early as 1 day following SE, the concentrations of NAA (−45.3%), glutamate (−35.1%) and GABA (−39.4%; all p<0.001) decreased substantially (Figure 3C,E,G) which was correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 3D,F,H; for NAA: r² = 0.89; for glutamate: r² = 0.93; for GABA: r² = 0.77; all p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 1H-MR spectroscopy shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance.

claim: Glutamate concentrations decreased substantially at 1 day following SE.
source: As early as 1 day following SE, the concentrations of NAA (−45.3%), glutamate (−35.1%) and GABA (−39.4%; all p<0.001) decreased substantially (Figure 3C,E,G) which was correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 3D,F,H; for NAA: r² = 0.89; for glutamate: r² = 0.93; for GABA: r² = 0.77; all p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 1H-MR spectroscopy shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance.

claim: GABA concentrations decreased substantially at 1 day following SE.
source: As early as 1 day following SE, the concentrations of NAA (−45.3%), glutamate (−35.1%) and GABA (−39.4%; all p<0.001) decreased substantially (Figure 3C,E,G) which was correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 3D,F,H; for NAA: r² = 0.89; for glutamate: r² = 0.93; for GABA: r² = 0.77; all p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 1H-MR spectroscopy shown in Figure 3G with statistical significance.

claim: Early NAA concentrations were correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis.
source: As early as 1 day following SE, the concentrations of NAA (−45.3%), glutamate (−35.1%) and GABA (−39.4%; all p<0.001) decreased substantially (Figure 3C,E,G) which was correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 3D,F,H; for NAA: r² = 0.89; for glutamate: r² = 0.93; for GABA: r² = 0.77; all p<0.001).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance.

claim: Early glutamate concentrations were correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis.
source: As early as 1 day following SE, the concentrations of NAA (−45.3%), glutamate (−35.1%) and GABA (−39.4%; all p<0.001) decreased substantially (Figure 3C,E,G) which was correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 3D,F,H; for NAA: r² = 0.89; for glutamate: r² = 0.93; for GABA: r² = 0.77; all p<0.001).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3F with statistical significance.

claim: Early GABA concentrations were correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis.
source: As early as 1 day following SE, the concentrations of NAA (−45.3%), glutamate (−35.1%) and GABA (−39.4%; all p<0.001) decreased substantially (Figure 3C,E,G) which was correlated with the later extent of cell death-associated microgliosis (Figure 3D,F,H; for NAA: r² = 0.89; for glutamate: r² = 0.93; for GABA: r² = 0.77; all p<0.001).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3H with statistical significance.

claim: The GCL width continuously increased at day 7, reaching significance at 14 and 21 days after SE when compared to controls.
source: Accordingly, quantitative analysis revealed a continuous increase of the GCL width at day 7, reaching significance at 14 and 21 days after SE when compared to controls (Figure 4A,B; control: 67.8 ± 2.5 µm; 14d: 132.6 ± 13.8 µm; 21d: 168.6 ± 9.9 µm, both p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance.

claim: Proximal dendrites of granule cells significantly thickened as early as day 7 after SE.
source: Furthermore, proximal dendrites significantly thickened as early as day 7 (control: 1.54 ± 0.04 µm, 7d: 1.86 ± 0.12 µm, p<0.05), while proximal axons increased in volume only during later stages of epileptogenesis at 14 and 21 days after SE (Figure 4C,D; control: 0.70 ± 0.02, 14d: 1.15 ± 0.08 µm; 21d: 1.63 ± 0.09 µm, both p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological analysis shown in Figure 4D with statistical significance.

claim: Proximal axons of granule cells increased in volume at 14 and 21 days after SE.
source: Furthermore, proximal dendrites significantly thickened as early as day 7 (control: 1.54 ± 0.04 µm, 7d: 1.86 ± 0.12 µm, p<0.05), while proximal axons increased in volume only during later stages of epileptogenesis at 14 and 21 days after SE (Figure 4C,D; control: 0.70 ± 0.02, 14d: 1.15 ± 0.08 µm; 21d: 1.63 ± 0.09 µm, both p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological analysis shown in Figure 4D with statistical significance.

claim: A significant increase of ZnT-3 was detected at 14 and 21 days after SE.
source: A few ZnT-3-labeled profiles were already evident at days 4 and 7 in the subgranular region, but a significant increase of ZnT-3 was only detected at 14 and 21 days after SE (Figure 4E,F; control: 4.02 ± 0.50, 14d: 11.64 ± 2.39, p>0.05; 21d: 14.57 ± 2.11, p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4F with statistical significance.

claim: The mean volume of radial glia processes significantly increased as early as 4 days after SE.
source: Interestingly, the mean volume of radial glia processes significantly increased as early as 4 days after SE (Figure 4G,H,I; control: 6.47 ± 1.15 µm³, 4d: 19.09 ± 0.55 µm³, p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative morphometry shown in Figure 4H-I with statistical significance.

claim: The optical density of GFAP was correlated with the size of the GCL in chronically epileptic mice.
source: Moreover, the optical density of GFAP was correlated with the size of the GCL in chronically epileptic mice (Figure 4M; r² = 0.89, p<0.0001), showing that radial gliosis is tightly associated with GCD.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 4M with statistical significance.

claim: Fractional anisotropy was increased in the dentate gyrus during late epileptogenesis.
source: Correspondingly, fractional anisotropy (as a measure of tissue organization) was increased in the DG during late epileptogenesis (Figure 5O; 16d: 19.9%, p<0.05; 31d: 28.1%, p<0.001), but exhibited an early and transient decrease in the CA1 region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G; 1d: −17.8%, p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DWI analysis shown in Figure 5O with statistical significance.

claim: Fractional anisotropy exhibited an early and transient decrease in the CA1 region.
source: Correspondingly, fractional anisotropy (as a measure of tissue organization) was increased in the DG during late epileptogenesis (Figure 5O; 16d: 19.9%, p<0.05; 31d: 28.1%, p<0.001), but exhibited an early and transient decrease in the CA1 region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G; 1d: −17.8%, p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DWI analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G with statistical significance.

claim: Axial diffusivity significantly increased as early as 8 days after SE in epileptic mice.
source: Particularly, the rise of AD during intermediate disease progression showed the most reliable correlation with chronic histopathological changes: AD significantly increased as early as 8 days after SE in epileptic mice (Figure 5M; 8d: 10.6%, p<0.01; 16d: 19.9%; 31d: 18.0%, both p<0.001) and was correlated with the volume of the GCL (Figure 5N; 8d: r² = 0.68, p<0.01; 16d: r² = 0.84, p<0.001; 31d: r² = 0.66, p<0.01), suggesting that AD is sensitive to microstructural alterations associated with GCD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DWI analysis shown in Figure 5M with statistical significance.

claim: Axial diffusivity was correlated with the volume of the GCL.
source: Particularly, the rise of AD during intermediate disease progression showed the most reliable correlation with chronic histopathological changes: AD significantly increased as early as 8 days after SE in epileptic mice (Figure 5M; 8d: 10.6%, p<0.01; 16d: 19.9%; 31d: 18.0%, both p<0.001) and was correlated with the volume of the GCL (Figure 5N; 8d: r² = 0.68, p<0.01; 16d: r² = 0.84, p<0.001; 31d: r² = 0.66, p<0.01), suggesting that AD is sensitive to microstructural alterations associated with GCD.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 5N with statistical significance.

claim: Dorsoventral diffusivity increased continuously reaching significance at day 8 after SE.
source: Indeed, dvD increased continuously reaching significance at day 8 (Figure 6F; 8d: 22.7%; 16d: 26.6%; 31d: 21.7%, all p<0.001) similar to the rise in AD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DWI analysis shown in Figure 6F with statistical significance.

claim: From 4 days onward the magnitude of dorsoventral diffusivity was highly correlated with the later GCL volume.
source: Importantly, from 4 days onward the magnitude of dvD as well as its calculated volume was highly correlated with the later GCL volume (Figure 6G) and the integrated density of GFAP labeling in the GCL (Figure 6J; 4d: r² = 0.61, p<0.01; 8d: r² = 0.85; 16d: r² = 0.87; 31d: r² = 0.81; all p<0.001).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 6G with statistical significance.

claim: From 4 days onward the magnitude of dorsoventral diffusivity was highly correlated with the integrated density of GFAP labeling in the GCL.
source: Importantly, from 4 days onward the magnitude of dvD as well as its calculated volume was highly correlated with the later GCL volume (Figure 6G) and the integrated density of GFAP labeling in the GCL (Figure 6J; 4d: r² = 0.61, p<0.01; 8d: r² = 0.85; 16d: r² = 0.87; 31d: r² = 0.81; all p<0.001).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 6J with statistical significance.

claim: Human epileptic hippocampi with strong hippocampal sclerosis exhibited elevated mean diffusivity and fractional anisotropy values in the dentate gyrus.
source: Similar to our results obtained in mice, human epileptic hippocampi with strong HS (i.e. Wyler grade III or IV) exhibited elevated MD and FA values in the DG, while FA was reduced in the CA1 region (Figure 7H–K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ex vivo DWI analysis of human tissue shown in Figure 7H-K.

claim: Fractional anisotropy was reduced in the CA1 region of human epileptic hippocampi with strong hippocampal sclerosis.
source: Similar to our results obtained in mice, human epileptic hippocampi with strong HS (i.e. Wyler grade III or IV) exhibited elevated MD and FA values in the DG, while FA was reduced in the CA1 region (Figure 7H–K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ex vivo DWI analysis of human tissue shown in Figure 7H-K.

claim: The density and volume of GFAP-labeled radial glia cell processes increased with the Wyler grade in human hippocampi.
source: Moreover, quantitative morphometry revealed that the density and volume of GFAP-labeled radial glia cell processes also increased with the Wyler grade (Figure 7L,N) demonstrating that radial gliosis accompanies HS also in humans.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative morphometry shown in Figure 7L,N.

claim: Fractional anisotropy values in the GCL were positively correlated with the density of radial glia processes in human hippocampi.
source: Importantly, FA values in the GCL were positively correlated with the density of radial glia processes (Figure 7P; r² = 0.78, p<0.05), suggesting that DWI biomarkers sensitive to microstructural changes in the DG are applicable in intractable mTLE in humans.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 7P with statistical significance.

claim: PC1 is strongly correlated with granule cell dispersion.
source: Mapping principal components (PCs) of the biomarker dataset onto histopathological changes associated with HS, we found a strong linear relationship between PC1 and GCD (r2 = 0.86, p<0.01), microgliosis (r2 = 0.68, p<0.05) and a trend for radial gliosis (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 8B with statistical significance.

claim: PC1 is strongly correlated with microgliosis.
source: Mapping principal components (PCs) of the biomarker dataset onto histopathological changes associated with HS, we found a strong linear relationship between PC1 and GCD (r2 = 0.86, p<0.01), microgliosis (r2 = 0.68, p<0.05) and a trend for radial gliosis (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 8C with statistical significance.

claim: PC1 is inversely correlated with seizure frequency.
source: Correlating the seizure frequency with PC1 revealed an inverse relationship between both parameters (Figure 9; r² = 0.94, p<0.01), suggesting that our identified biomarkers are also predictive for the seizure severity in chronically epileptic mice.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 9C with statistical significance.

claim: More severe early hippocampal injury and subsequent tissue reorganization lead to the development of stronger hippocampal sclerosis and lower seizure burden.
source: This data indicates that more severe early hippocampal injury and subsequent tissue reorganization lead to the development of stronger HS and lower seizure burden, compared to a milder, but still epileptogenic insult.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inverse correlation between PC1 and seizure frequency.

claim: Radial gliosis largely affects early diffusivity changes in the dentate gyrus.
source: Our results are in line with Budde et al. (2011) and Salo et al. (2017) showing that FA increases with glial scarring in the perilesional cortex following cerebral trauma or the CA3 region following SE, respectively. The notion that changes in DWI metrics are influenced by gliosis is further supported by our observation that DWI changes in the DG were accompanied by T2 hyperintensity, known to correlate best with the number of local glia cells (Briellmann et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by correlations between DWI metrics and GFAP density shown in Figure 6, and cited literature.

claim: T2-weighted imaging and 1H-MR spectroscopy are useful tools for early prognosis (1–4 days after the precipitating insult) of later epilepsy severity.
source: In summary, our PCA results corroborate the idea that T2-weighted imaging and 1H-MR spectroscopy are useful tools for early prognosis (1–4 days after the precipitating insult) of later epilepsy severity, whereas DWI is informative at subsequent stages of disease development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: DWI is informative at subsequent stages of disease development.
source: In summary, our PCA results corroborate the idea that T2-weighted imaging and 1H-MR spectroscopy are useful tools for early prognosis (1–4 days after the precipitating insult) of later epilepsy severity, whereas DWI is informative at subsequent stages of disease development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 8.
